lesson.grammar_point: how much / how many + some / any (countable and uncountable)

listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to the Bastille market. Here is some information for today. We are open from seven in the morning to half past two. How much is the bread? One baguette is one euro twenty, and a big loaf is two euros fifty. The cheese is at the third table on the left. How many pieces do you want? One small piece is about six euros. We have some apples from the south of France today, and they are very cheap: five euros for one kilo. We don't have any strawberries this week, sorry. You can pay with a credit card at every table. Thank you, and have a very good Saturday.

Hello, this is a message from the cheese shop on Rue Paul Bert. You asked about our prices, so here they are. A small piece of cheese is six euros. A big piece is eleven euros. If you want some cheese for a family of three, one big piece is enough. We also have some bread, but not much, and only in the morning. How many people are coming to your dinner? Call us and we can prepare a box for you. One more thing: on Sunday we are closed, so please come on Saturday. We open at eight and we close at one. Thank you very much.

reading.rtitle: Saturday at the Market -- A Morning in Paris
paras: On Saturday morning the Bastille market opens at seven o'clock. It is one of the biggest markets in Paris, on one long street near the metro station.
The bread is very good and it is cheap. One baguette is about one euro twenty. The cheese is more expensive: a small piece can be six euros.
Many families come early, before nine. You hear the same two questions all morning: "How much is the bread?" and "How many apples do you want?"
The people at the market don't always speak English, but they always understand numbers. You can say "two, please" and show two fingers. It works every time.
The market closes at half past two. After two o'clock some prices go down, because the food can't stay on the table until Monday.
